```{r}
source('../01_code/reporting.R')
DS <- fread(file.path(OUT,'tables/descriptives.csv'))
```

This supplement accompanies *Do socio-emotional skills transmit socioeconomic advantage? Evidence from PISA 2025 data*. It retains all estimable systems, including incomplete skill blocks, and documents the models behind the country estimates. Figures and tables read the saved global mediation results. No regression was rerun to prepare this draft.

**Reading conventions.** Brackets after estimates are 95% uncertainty intervals, combining school-bootstrap and plausible-value variation. SES units are ten national percentile-rank points; deprivation units are additional unaffordable items at given individual and school ESCS. Skill gradients are in country-specific standard deviations. Country labels identify the source population, including subnational samples. Main-paper comparisons use all six skills; other blocks are explicitly marked. A missing skill coefficient is shown as a dash, never zero. Tables here are numbered independently of those in the manuscript.

# Sample and measurement coverage

The source has 90 systems. SES models are estimable in 82 and deprivation models in 75. The common-six-skill subsets contain 69 and 63 systems. Eligibility depends on observed variables, valid weights, at least 100 complete pupils and 30 schools; the main subset additionally requires all six skills. Within the eligible systems, models for an exposure use a common complete-case sample across all skill and achievement equations.

\clearpage

```{r}
#| results: asis
c <- merge(A[exposure=='SES' & status=='Eligible',.(CNT,economy,N,schools,skills,complete_share)],
           A[exposure=='DEP',.(CNT,depN=ifelse(status=='Eligible',N,NA_integer_),items)],by='CNT')
c <- c[order(economy)]
x <- c[,.(Code=CNT,System=economy,Skills=skills,`SES N`=num(N),Schools=num(schools),
           `Complete %`=fmt(100*complete_share,1),`DEP N`=ifelse(is.na(depN),'—',num(depN)),Items=ifelse(is.na(depN),'—',items))]
tbl(x,'Country coverage. Complete percent is the SES analytic share of the source pupil count; DEP N is its complete-deprivation subset. Schools refers to the SES sample.',7.2,widths=c(NA,'3.5cm',NA,NA,NA,NA,NA,NA))
```

The retained deprivation count uses nine candidate items. For a system, a candidate is retained when at least 90% of respondents who answer any candidate provide a valid response. A count requires responses to every retained item. Only response 2 (“No, cannot afford it”) counts as deprivation; responses 1 and 3 count zero. Equal item counts need not imply equal definitions. The source bundle contains `deprivation_item_sets.csv` and the item dictionary, together with the detailed response-coverage audit.

```{r}
#| results: asis
x<-A[exposure=='DEP' & status=='Eligible',.(Systems=.N,`Six-skill systems`=sum(skills==6)),by=.(Items=items)][order(Items)]
tbl(x,'Deprivation coverage by number of retained items. The main six-skill sample has 13 distinct item sets.',9)
```

The eight systems lacking an SES model are listed below. Seven further systems with estimable SES models lack a deprivation model: Argentina, Germany, Israel, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and Norway. These are measurement or model-input exclusions, not decisions based on results.

```{r}
#| results: asis
tbl(A[exposure=='SES' & status!='Eligible',.(Code=CNT,System=economy,Reason=status)][order(System)],
    'Systems without an SES model.',8,widths=c(NA,'3.5cm','10.5cm'))
```

## Country descriptives

The next table reports weighted means on the SES analytic sample and the mean deprivation count on the deprivation analytic sample. The reading mean averages the ten plausible values. The reading SD describes the pupil-level average of those values, not the latent proficiency SD. Rank is divided by ten, with approximate support 0--10. Complete descriptive statistics (N, mean, SD, minimum, maximum) for every available skill, exposure and control, separately by country and exposure, are supplied in `tables/descriptives.csv`. Skills have weighted mean zero and SD one by construction on the SES sample; the deprivation subset uses those same transformations.

```{r}
#| results: asis
ids<-A[exposure=='SES' & status=='Eligible'][order(economy),CNT]
xx<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc) {
 f<-function(v,ex='SES') {z<-DS[CNT==cc & variable==v & exposure==ex];if(nrow(z)) paste0(fmt(z$mean,2),' (',fmt(z$SD,2),')') else '—'}
 data.table(Code=cc,System=G[CNT==cc,economy],Reading=f('Reading'),Rank=f('SES_rank'),ESCS=f('ESCS'),Deprivation=f('DEP','DEP'))
}))
tbl(xx,'Country means (standard deviations), weighted by final student weights. Deprivation uses its own analytic sample.',7.5,widths=c(NA,'3.5cm',NA,NA,NA,NA))
```

# Exact estimands and R specifications

## Models and units

For every exposure and system, the outcome is reading and the available skills enter jointly. Let `status` denote rank/10 or deprivation. Every variable is split into its weighted school mean (`_B`) and deviation from that mean (`_W`). The school intercept is random and all slopes are fixed within a country. There is no random grade slope, school fixed-effect-only regression, or pooled cross-country coefficient in this analysis.

The specifications below show the full six-skill SES case. They are executable model formulas, but this document does not run them. In deprivation models the control vector additionally contains `ESCS_W` and `ESCS_B`. Norway omits age where unavailable. In partial-block systems, the same model includes only the measured skills.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
skills <- c('PERSEV','CURIO','ENPROBS','COGABIL','GOALSET','SELFREG')
controls <- c('nonmale','AGE')
if (exposure == 'DEP') controls <- c(controls,'ESCS')

# Two-level survey weights; school_weight is W_NRASCHBWT.
d[, w1 := W_FSTUWT / school_weight]
d[, w1 := w1 * .N / sum(w1), by = school]
# w2 is school_weight divided by a country-specific constant.
for (v in c('status', controls, skills)) {
  d[, (paste0(v,'_B')) := weighted.mean(get(v), w1), by=school]
  d[, (paste0(v,'_W')) := get(v) - get(paste0(v,'_B'))]
}
wb <- function(v) c(paste0(v,'_W'), paste0(v,'_B'))
f_m1 <- reformulate(c(wb('status'), wb(controls), '(1|school)'),
                   response='CURIO')  # repeat for every skill
f_m0 <- reformulate(c(wb('status'), wb(controls), '(1|school)'),
                   response='PV1READ')
f_m2 <- reformulate(c(wb('status'), wb(controls), wb(skills),
                     '(1|school)'), response='PV1READ')
# Repeat M0 and M2 for PV1READ ... PV10READ.
m1 <- WeMix::mix(f_m1, data=d, weights=c('w1','w2'), cWeights=TRUE)
m2 <- WeMix::mix(f_m2, data=d, weights=c('w1','w2'), cWeights=TRUE)
f_s <- reformulate(c('status',controls,paste0(controls,'_B')),
                  response='status_B')
sorting <- lm(f_s, data=d, weights=W_FSTUWT)
delta <- coef(sorting)[['status']]
# Sensitivity only: same formula, unweighted maximum likelihood.
m2_unweighted <- lme4::lmer(f_m2, data=d, REML=FALSE)
```

**What a and b mean.** In M1, `status_W` and `status_B` supply $a_W$ and $a_B$: skill SD per exposure unit. In M2, each skill's `_W` and `_B` supply $b_W$ and $b_B$: reading points per skill SD after controlling for all other skills. M2's `status_W` and `status_B` supply $c'_W$ and $c'_B$. M0 supplies the reading gradients before skills. S supplies $\delta$, the individual-to-school exposure projection.

The fitted main engine evaluates this Gaussian weighted likelihood using school sufficient statistics and profiles the variance components. It was checked against direct WeMix fits. No `mediate()` object is involved. The joint mediation contrast is computed from the model coefficients for each plausible value, and uncertainty comes from refitting the complete sequence on resampled schools.

## Why coefficient products give the joint contrast

Write the expected reading outcome at exposure profile $x$ as an additive function of the skill vector. Hold the outcome exposure profile at $x_1$ and compare predictions integrating over two joint skill distributions, $G_1$ and $G_0$, corresponding to the higher and lower exposure profiles. Then

$$
\begin{split}
I_S&=E\{Y(x_1,M\sim G_1)\}-E\{Y(x_1,M\sim G_0)\}\\
&=\sum_k b_{Wk}\Delta E(M^W_k)+\sum_k b_{Bk}\Delta E(\bar M_k)\\
&=(1-\delta)\sum_k a_{Wk}b_{Wk}+\delta\sum_k a_{Bk}b_{Bk}.
\end{split}
$$

The equality follows from linearity of the outcome expectation and the fitted M1 gradients. Correlation among skills does not alter this additive expectation. It would matter differently in a model with interactions or nonlinear links. The calculation is related to joint interventional mediation, rather than six unrelated single-mediator natural-effect analyses [@vansteelandt2017; @imai2010].

$\delta$ is a calibration for the observed profile comparison. It does not define a feasible randomized school-assignment intervention, identify peer effects or allocate the school contrast between formation and selection. The main paper's Research limitations section states the identification conditions for a causal interpretation. In particular, a within--between decomposition distinguishes levels without making allocation random.

The within pathway $I_W$ holds the school context fixed. The between pathway $I_B$ is per unit of school-average exposure. The quantities are not added unweighted. The sorting addition is $\Delta_S=\delta(I_B-I_W)$. The remaining component is $D=(1-\delta)c'_W+\delta c'_B$, and the denominator is $T=D+I_S$, not the M0 coefficient. Each skill contribution sums within the same joint model. Negative contributions are preserved.

Shares are reported only when the total interval excludes zero, plausible-value totals retain their sign, bootstrap/plausible-value denominator signs agree at least 99%, and the components support the same proportional interpretation. Unstable or offsetting decompositions retain reading-point estimates but withhold percentages. The source `ratio_audit.csv` records the decision and reason for every country. Percentages are averaged over plausible values, so they can differ slightly from the ratio of the printed averaged point estimates.

## Worked regression-to-pathway example

The table links the two regressions to a skill contribution, using curiosity. The $a$ columns come from M1; the $b$ columns come from M2 with all six skills. $I_{S,k}$ combines both levels with S. For Denmark, the within curiosity product is about `r fmt(est('DNK','indW_CURIO'))` reading points; its total profile contribution is `r fmt(est('DNK','indS_CURIO'))` points. Korea has a positive within SES gradient in curiosity but no clearly positive joint curiosity pathway. A social gradient alone is therefore insufficient.

```{r}
#| results: asis
xx<-rbindlist(lapply(c('DNK','KOR','MYS'),function(cc) {
 rbindlist(lapply(c('aW_CURIO','aB_CURIO','bW_CURIO','bB_CURIO','indS_CURIO'),function(tt)
 data.table(System=G[CNT==cc,economy],Quantity=sub('_CURIO','',tt),`Estimate [95% CI]`=ci(cc,tt,digits=3))))
}))
tbl(xx,'Curiosity: linking M1, M2 and the sorting profile. SES exposure; three illustrative systems with all six skills.',9)
```

## Inference and validation

Every country--exposure job uses 499 valid whole-school bootstrap draws. A draw refits M0, all M1 skill equations, M2 for all ten plausible values, and S; the uncertainty of $\delta$ and of both mediation links is therefore included. With $P=10$, the pooled variance is $\bar U+(1+1/P)B$, where $\bar U$ is the mean bootstrap variance across plausible values and $B$ is their point-estimate variance. The interval is the pooled mean plus or minus 1.96 pooled standard errors. Rank and skill standardization are held at their prepared values during this bootstrap.

The school resampling is an exploratory cluster-bootstrap approximation, not PISA's full stratified two-stage BRR procedure. The same inference convention is applied to all systems. Multiple-testing adjustments use approximate two-sided normal p-values. The retained families comprise all available within/between skill gradients by exposure, all individual skill contributions by exposure, and the joint pathway/sorting-addition family by exposure. The six-skill tables retain these full-analysis adjustments rather than recalculating a smaller family after selection on coverage.

The archived pilot replication reproduced Denmark, Korea and Malaysia's earlier point estimates and standard errors exactly. Direct WeMix verification of ten additional deprivation cases had a maximum fixed-coefficient discrepancy of $4.32\times10^{-6}$. The copied validation files record those numerical checks and input checks. Estimation used WeMix 4.0.3 and lme4 1.1.37; package versions and the original R session information are included in the bundle.

# Joint country results

For a ten-rank-point SES comparison, $I_W$ is the predicted reading difference carried by skills with school setting fixed; $I_S$ includes the school component associated with that family difference. $\Delta_S$ is their difference. For deprivation, the same columns concern one additional unaffordable item, with ESCS held constant at both levels. All entries are reading points; they are not skill SD, percentages or coefficients on school SES itself.

```{r}
#| results: asis
for(ex in c('SES','DEP')) {
 ids<-A[exposure==ex & status=='Eligible'][order(economy),CNT]
 xx<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc) data.table(Code=cc,System=G[CNT==cc,economy],
   K=A[CNT==cc & exposure==ex,skills],IW=ci(cc,'skills_same_school',ex),
   IS=ci(cc,'skills_sorting',ex),Addition=ci(cc,'sorting_increment',ex))))
 print(tbl(xx,paste0(if(ex=='SES')'Socioeconomic rank' else 'Material deprivation',': joint skills pathways in every estimable system. K is the observed skill count; K = 6 is the main-paper sample.'),7.2,
   widths=c(NA,'3.0cm',NA,'3.0cm','3.0cm','3.0cm')))
}
```

## Total and remaining gradients

The model-implied total $T$ includes the skills pathway $I_S$ and remaining component $D$. A share is printed only where it passes the pre-specified denominator checks above. For example, Malaysia's deprivation total is `r ci('MYS','total','DEP')` points, with a skills pathway of `r ci('MYS','skills_sorting','DEP')` and a remaining component of `r ci('MYS','remaining','DEP')`. Neither the remaining component nor the entire school gradient is labelled a skills effect.

```{r}
#| results: asis
for(ex in c('SES','DEP')) {
 ids<-A[exposure==ex & status=='Eligible'][order(economy),CNT]
 xx<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc) data.table(Code=cc,System=G[CNT==cc,economy],
    Total=ci(cc,'total',ex),Remaining=ci(cc,'remaining',ex),
    `Skills share %`=if(R[CNT==cc & exposure==ex,share_reportable])ci(cc,'share',ex,1) else 'Withheld')))
 print(tbl(xx,paste0(ex,': model-implied total, remaining component and admissible skills share.'),7.4,
    widths=c(NA,'3.4cm','3.4cm','3.4cm','3.4cm')))
}
```

# Individual skill contributions

The following tables retain the skill-specific pathways for all systems. Each cell is $I_{S,k}$, a contribution in reading points, with its interval. Because M2 contains the entire observed skill block, a partial-block coefficient need not equal the corresponding six-skill coefficient that would be obtained if the missing scales existed. Dashes are missing measures. The machine-readable `input/estimates.csv` contains all $a_W,a_B,b_W,b_B$, within, between and sorting-profile contributions, sampling and plausible-value uncertainty, p-values and adjusted q-values.

```{r}
#| results: asis
for(ex in c('SES','DEP')) {
 ids<-A[exposure==ex & status=='Eligible'][order(economy),CNT]
 xx<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc) {
   z<-data.table(Code=cc)
   for(k in names(sklab)) z[,(k):=if(nrow(E[CNT==cc & exposure==ex & term==paste0('indS_',k)]))ci(cc,paste0('indS_',k),ex,1) else '—']
   z
 }))
 print(tbl(xx,paste0(ex,': individual skill contributions, including the school sorting component. Column codes are defined below.'),7.0,
      widths=c('1.2cm',rep('2.25cm',6))))
}
```

PERSEV = perseverance; CURIO = curiosity; ENPROBS = enjoyment of problem solving; COGABIL = cognitive adaptability; GOALSET = goal setting; SELFREG = self-regulated learning. Country codes map to full names in the coverage table.

# RQ2 and RQ3: between-school links

The main-text two-link figure displays within-school coefficients. This companion retains the between-school coefficients from the same six-skill models. The horizontal axis is the skill difference per ten school-average rank points; the vertical axis is the reading difference per unit of school-average skill, with the other skills included. Skill units remain standard deviations of the pupil-level country distribution; the school means are not restandardized. Their product is the skill's between-school contribution before weighting by the sorting coefficient. It is not the full individual-profile contribution, which also contains the within-school term.

![Between-school skill gradients and reading relationships in all 69 six-skill systems. Dashed curves mark products of 1, 3 and 5 reading points, from lower to higher curves. Equal products can arise from different combinations of the two links. These are point estimates, not tests of cross-country differences.](../04_output/figures/ses_gap_link_b.pdf){width=100% fig-pos='H'}

# RQ1: evidence by skill and level

RQ1 concerns the exposure-to-skill gradient. The next tables count evidence in the direction suggested by the resource argument at each level: positive for SES and negative for deprivation. “Opposite” is the reverse direction; “uncertain” includes zero. The denominator is 69 for SES and 63 for deprivation throughout these tables. BH support uses the full-analysis adjustment family, not a fresh within-subset correction.

```{r}
#| results: asis
for(ex in c('SES','DEP')) {
 z<-H[scope=='Six-skill systems only' & exposure==ex & grepl('^a[WB]_',term)]
 zz<-z[,.(Support=sum(classification=='Supports'),Opposite=sum(classification=='Opposite'),
       Uncertain=sum(classification=='Inconclusive'),`BH support`=sum(adjusted_support)),by=term]
 zz[,Level:=ifelse(grepl('^aW_',term),'Within','Between')]
 zz[,Skill:=unname(sklab[sub('^a[WB]_','',term)])]
 print(tbl(zz[order(Skill,Level),.(Skill,Level,Support,Opposite,Uncertain,`BH support`)],
     paste0(ex,': evidence for the social gradient in each skill.'),8))
}
```

The manuscript's joint-pathway summary is based on intervals for the entire calculated contrast. It does not require each component to be individually significant, and it does not infer a country difference merely because one interval excludes zero and another does not.

# Sensitivity results

## Visual comparison of deprivation specifications

![Joint deprivation pathway under the main and alternative specifications. All eligible six-skill systems are retained in each panel: 63 for weight scaling, minimum school sample size and unweighted lmer; 61 for the common-four-item definition. Both axes use reading points per additional unaffordable item, with identical scales. Country labels identify the three largest absolute changes per panel and map to the coverage table. The diagonal denotes agreement, not statistical significance.](../04_output/figures/dep_robustness.pdf){width=100% fig-pos='H'}

Changing to four common items changes the exposure definition while retaining the same pupils within each system. It is therefore a measurement comparison, not simply another estimator of an unchanged item count. The unweighted lmer comparison retains the main sorting coefficient. All plotted alternatives were saved in the original analysis; this display adds no model fits or bootstrap intervals.

## Weighting, sample and deprivation measurement

These saved sensitivity estimates were produced in the original analysis. They are point-estimate comparisons without new bootstrap intervals. Unscaled weights change the conditional weight normalization; minimum-10 excludes schools with fewer than ten analytic pupils. The unweighted `lmer()` comparison retains the main sorting coefficient, isolating the change in the mixed-model estimation. For deprivation, the core-four analysis uses the same pupils but changes the exposure definition. The SES-on-deprivation-sample analysis uses rank, not deprivation: its appropriate comparator is the main SES estimate.

```{r}
#| results: asis
for(ex in c('SES','DEP')) {
 ids<-A[exposure==ex & status=='Eligible' & skills==6][order(economy),CNT]
 xx<-rbindlist(lapply(ids,function(cc) {
   getv<-function(v) {z<-V[CNT==cc & exposure==ex & variant==v & term=='skills_sorting',estimate];if(length(z))fmt(z) else '—'}
   z<-data.table(Code=cc,Main=fmt(est(cc,'skills_sorting',ex)),Unscaled=getv('unscaled_weights'),
       `Min. 10`=getv('minimum_10'),Unweighted=fmt(L[CNT==cc & exposure==ex & term=='skills_sorting',lmer_unweighted]))
   if(ex=='DEP')z[,`Core four`:=getv('core_four_same_sample')]
   if(ex=='SES') {v<-V[CNT==cc & exposure=='DEP' & variant=='SES_on_deprivation_sample' & term=='skills_sorting',estimate];z[,`DEP sample`:=if(length(v))fmt(v) else '—']}
   z
 }))
 print(tbl(xx,paste0(ex,': sensitivity of the joint skills point estimate, full-six-skill systems. A dash means the alternative is unavailable.'),8))
}
```

Malaysia illustrates why the weighting choice is substantive. Its unweighted SES pathway is about half the weighted estimate, while Korea's remains large. Denmark's rank pathway is close under the two estimators, but this does not justify treating all country results as weight-invariant. The core-four deprivation comparison also changes the exposure itself; agreement in sign is useful, but equality of magnitude is not expected.

## Omitted-variable stress tests

The saved stress test perturbs the fitted skill--outcome relationship in a deliberately adverse residual direction. For level $\ell$, define $K_\ell=s_{Y\ell}\sqrt{a_\ell'\Sigma_\ell^{-1}a_\ell}$, where $\Sigma_\ell$ is the full residual covariance of skills. The perturbation is

$$I_\ell(\rho)=I_\ell(0)-\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}K_\ell.$$

The sign of $\rho$ is chosen to move the original estimate towards zero, and the curve is allowed to cross zero. The profile calculation combines the within and between scales using $(1-\delta)$ and $\delta$. The between component conditions on fitted effective GLS weights. This is a fixed-projection omitted-bias stress test. It is not a complete multilevel `medsens()` analysis, an estimated bias correction, or a test of exposure--mediator confounding. A larger threshold means a larger perturbation is needed under this particular construction, not that all causal identification concerns are small.

```{r}
#| results: asis
ss<-read_input('sensitivity_thresholds')
xx<-merge(ss[level=='S'],A[status=='Eligible' & skills==6,.(CNT,exposure,economy)],by=c('CNT','exposure'))
tbl(xx[order(exposure,economy),.(Exposure=exposure,Code=CNT,`Point-zero |rho|`=fmt(point_zero_rho,3),
    `First |rho| with CI at zero`=fmt(first_grid_rho_CI_includes_zero,2))],
    'Residual-confounding stress thresholds for the joint skills pathway. Zero in the final column means the original interval already includes zero.',8)
```

The archived diagnostics also include an own-observation-excluded school-mean check for the sorting projection. This changes that calibration only, not every contextual equation. It should not be read as a complete leave-one-out re-estimation of mediation.

# Incomplete skill blocks

The 13 additional SES systems and 12 additional deprivation systems broaden the geographical coverage. Their estimates answer the question for the observed skill vector. A smaller block is not a lower bound on the six-skill pathway, since adding correlated mediators can change both individual contributions and their sum.

![SES pathways in systems with incomplete skill blocks. Braces give the number of skills measured. These estimates are retained for scope assessment and are outside the common-six-skill comparison.](../04_output/figures/ses_pathways_partial.pdf){width=100% fig-pos='H'}

![Deprivation pathways in systems with incomplete skill blocks. Brackets give deprivation items and braces the measured skill count. The same exposure and uncertainty conventions apply.](../04_output/figures/dep_pathways_partial.pdf){width=100% fig-pos='H'}

# Research bundle and provenance

The `ijed_ses_seg` routine has three parts: immutable copied aggregate inputs; reproducible reporting and figure code; and editable Quarto manuscripts with BibTeX references. The source manifest records original locations and SHA-256 hashes. Descriptives were computed from saved analytic RDS inputs without refitting. The deliverable contains those aggregate descriptives, not pupil-level files.

`render.R` generates the figures and two PDFs from the saved results. It never calls an estimator. `01_descriptives.R` is optional and requires the original analytic inputs to regenerate the descriptive table. The original estimation scripts are archived separately for inspection; they preserve the preceding analysis workflow and its input requirements. Numerical checks verify component sums, sorting identities, coverage counts, figure coverage, interval fields and the copied-file hashes. This is a new reporting routine, leaving the previous Paper A and global reports unchanged.
